entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5092"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 30</title> <div sID="gen7555" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.30.1-Job.30.31">Job 30:1-31</reference>.<div eID="gen7555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7556" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5092"/><hi type="bold">1. younger--</hi>not the three friends (<reference osisRef="Job.15.10">Job 15:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.32.4">32:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.6.7">6, 7</reference>). A general description: <reference osisRef="Job.30.1-Job.30.8">Job 30:1-8</reference>, the lowness of the persons who derided him; <reference osisRef="Job.30.9-Job.30.15">Job 30:9-15</reference>, the derision itself. Formerly old men rose to me (<reference osisRef="Job.29.8">Job 29:8</reference>). Now not only my juniors, who are bound to reverence me (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">Le 19:32</reference>), but even the mean and base-born actually deride me; opposed to, "smiled upon" (<reference osisRef="Job.29.24">Job 29:24</reference>). This goes farther than even the "mockery" of Job by relations and friends (<reference osisRef="Job.12.4">Job 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.10">16:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.16.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.2">17:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.17.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.22">19:22</reference>). Orientals feel keenly any indignity shown by the young. Job speaks as a rich Arabian emir, proud of his descent.<div eID="gen7556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dogs--</hi>regarded with disgust in the East as unclean (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.43">1Sa 17:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.11">Pr 26:11</reference>). They are not allowed to enter a house, but run about wild in the open air, living on offal and chance morsels (<reference osisRef="Ps.59.14">Psa 59:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.59.15">15</reference>). Here again we are reminded of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>). "Their fathers, my coevals, were so mean and famished that I would not have associated them with (not to say, set them over) my dogs in guarding my flock." <div eID="gen7557" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 30 Job 30:1-31 . 1. younger-- not the three friends ( Job 15:10 ; 32:4 , 6, 7 ). A general description: Job 30:1-8 , the lowness of the persons who derided him; Job 30:9-15 , the derision itself. Formerly old men rose to me ( Job 29:8 ). Now not only my juniors, who are bound to reverence me ( Le 19:32 ), but even the mean and base-born actually deride me; opposed to, "smiled upon" ( Job 29:24 ). This goes farther than even the "mockery" of Job by relations and friends ( Job 12:4 ; 16:10 , 20 ; 17:2 , 6 ; 19:22 ). Orientals feel keenly any indignity shown by the young. Job speaks as a rich Arabian emir, proud of his descent. dogs-- regarded with disgust in the East as unclean ( 1Sa 17:43 ; Pr 26:11 ). They are not allowed to enter a house, but run about wild in the open air, living on offal and chance morsels ( Psa 59:14 , 15 ). Here again we are reminded of Jesus Christ ( Psa 22:16 ). "Their fathers, my coevals, were so mean and famished that I would not have associated them with (not to say, set them over) my dogs in guarding my flock."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5093"/><div sID="gen7558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5093"/>2. If their fathers could be of no profit to me, much less the sons, who are feebler than their sires; and in whose case the hope of attaining old age is utterly gone, so puny are they (<reference osisRef="Job.5.26">Job 5:26</reference>) [Maurer]. Even if they had "strength of hands," that could be now of no use to me, as all I want in my present affliction is sympathy. <div eID="gen7558" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5114"/><div sID="gen7603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5114"/><hi type="bold">24. Expressing Job's faith as to the state after death. Though one must go to the grave, yet He will no more afflict in the ruin of the body (so Hebrew for "grave") there, if one has cried to Him when being destroyed. The "stretching of His hand" to punish after death answers antithetically to the raising "the cry" of prayer in the second clause. Maurer gives another translation which accords with the scope of <reference osisRef="Job.30.24-Job.30.31">Job 30:24-31</reference>; if it be natural for one in affliction to ask aid, why should it be considered (by the friends) wrong in my case? "Nevertheless does not a man in ruin stretch out his hand" (imploring help, <reference osisRef="Job.30.20">Job 30:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.17">La 1:17</reference>)? If one be in his calamity (destruction) is there not therefore a "cry" (for aid)? Thus in the parallelism "cry" answers to "stretch--</hi>hand"; "in his calamity," to "in ruin." The negative of the first clause is to be supplied in the second, as in <reference osisRef="Job.30.25">Job 30:25</reference> (<reference osisRef="Job.28.17">Job 28:17</reference>). <div eID="gen7603" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5119"/><div sID="gen7612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5119"/><hi type="bold">29. dragons ... owls--</hi>rather, "jackals," "ostriches," both of which utter dismal screams (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.8">Mi 1:8</reference>); in which respect, as also in their living amidst solitudes (the emblem of desolation), Job is their brother and companion; that is, resembles them. "Dragon," Hebrew, tannim, usually means the crocodile; so perhaps here, its open jaws lifted towards heaven, and its noise making it seem as if it mourned over its fate [Bochart]. <div eID="gen7612" type="x-p"/>
